readings.title: A map of public toilets
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A city published a map of public toilets. Visitors found several markers, but some facilities were closed outside the hours shown online. The main obstacle was opening times that were not maintained. Different departments updated signs and the website on separate schedules. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of map entries and site notices. Staff checked locations and contacted managers responsible for each facility. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a shared update routine improved reliability. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced dated map entries with one reporting channel. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: public data is useful only while it stays current. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a map of public toilets, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Comparing neighbourhood recycling rates
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community group compared recycling totals by neighbourhood. The largest area appeared most successful simply because it had more households. The main obstacle was raw totals presented without a fair denominator. Readers were not told how many homes contributed to each figure. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a calculation using households served. Analysts checked collection coverage and displayed both totals and rates. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated the ranking changed after adjustment. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a chart explaining what each number measures. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: data comparisons need the right scale. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in comparing neighbourhood recycling rates, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A walking map for visitors
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A museum published a walking map of nearby landmarks. First-time visitors missed a turning because a small footpath looked like a main road. The main obstacle was map symbols that were too similar. The route key relied on subtle shades that blurred in printed copies. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a trial with unfamiliar map readers. Designers watched visitors trace the route without offering spoken directions. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated clear line styles prevented wrong turns. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised key with landmarks and contrasting paths. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: maps must communicate choices at a glance. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a walking map for visitors, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Understanding a public spending chart
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town posted a chart of annual service spending. Residents thought one service had lost funding because the graph began above zero. The main obstacle was a truncated axis that exaggerated change. The bars made a small difference look dramatic without explaining the scale. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a chart review with community readers. The finance team compared interpretations of the first graph with a version starting at zero. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated the full scale gave a fairer impression. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a corrected chart with exact figures and notes. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: transparent data requires honest presentation. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in understanding a public spending chart, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for public data and map communication must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the open data learning programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于公共数据与地图表达的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the civic data team about a community activity related to public data and map communication. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the open data learning programme. People have noticed opening times that were not maintained, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
